name: Adam Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do nights at a big twenty-four-hour hypermarket off the ring road. From ten till about two I'm on the one staffed till plus the self-checkout bank, and after that I switch to picking online orders with a handheld scanner, running a trolley round the aisles. I've only been there eight months, so I still get the frozen aisle wrong and the scanner tells me off. It's a weird, quiet world at three in the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about nights, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that nobody's breathing down my neck, and I can listen to podcasts while I pick, mostly about tech and politics. What wears me out is the body clock, I'm basically jet-lagged all week. I share a flat with my mate Dev, who's a junior developer, and we see each other for about ten minutes a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is that the tech is cool but the bosses oversell it to shareholders. At work I'd joke that the picking app still can't find the oat milk. Online I'd post something a bit nerdy about why the hype didn't land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, for me it'd mean stability, which isn't bad. I already use AI every day, for my budget, for planning meals, even to draft emails to my landlord. If it stays a handy helper, I keep my night shifts and keep learning on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and start an evening course in electrics or IT support, because I want to be the guy fixing the self-checkouts, not standing next to them. I'd keep putting about a hundred and twenty a month into savings. And I'd keep nudging the night crew to join the union, because nights get forgotten.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, I think. A bit bored, maybe, because I like it when things move. But calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nights get forgotten. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The day staff get the meetings, the training, the free pizza when targets are hit. We find out about changes from a note taped on the fridge. If anything ever does get cut, nights would hear about it last, which is why I want us organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes, how long would you stay on nights?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two more years, until the course is done. Nights pay a bit extra, which helps the savings, but I don't want to be thirty and still eating breakfast at six in the evening. The plan is days, and a job with a toolbox.

say: I'd joke at work that the **picking app** still can't find the oat milk.
I'd post online that bosses **oversell the tech** to shareholders.
think: Privately, a **plateau** means stability, and I keep my night shifts.
I already use AI daily for **budgeting and emails**, so a helper suits me.
do: Start an **evening course** in electrics or IT support.
Keep saving about **£120 a month** toward my cushion.
Keep nudging the night crew to join the **union**.
feel: **Calm**, and a little **bored** because I like change.
S0.quote: I want to be the guy fixing the self-checkouts, not standing next to them.
fieldNote: Adam is a daily **AI user** and treats the tools as helpers, not threats.
He already plans a move toward **technical work** even when nothing changes.
His progressive streak shows in organising the **night shift**, who he feels get overlooked.

steps.text: Keep the night shifts on tills and online picking
Enrol in an evening electrics or IT support course
Save about a hundred and twenty a month
Sign up two night colleagues to the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get trained, not to hide. To friends I'd say the companies should pay for that training out of what they save. Online I'd probably share guides on free AI courses, because I'm that guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my till isn't the first thing to go, the thinking work is. The online orders already get planned by software, the substitutions get picked by software. What worries me is that the robots for picking, the little ones on rails, come in slowly and nights are where they'd test them first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager this month if I can shadow the engineer who services the self-checkouts and the picking scanners. I'd finish the IT support certificate within a year. I'd also use AI to build a proper CV, because mine is one line of school and three lines of shop jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but kind of excited. It's like the game changed the rules, and I'm young enough to learn them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on nights would struggle in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mick, who runs the bakery ovens at four in the morning. He's fifty-five, he hates phones, and he calls the app the gremlin. I'd honestly try to teach Mick the basics, but I don't know if he'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the engineer job never opens up at your store?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look outside. The self-checkouts and picking scanners are serviced by an outside firm, and it covers dozens of shops. My till isn't the first thing to go, the thinking work is. The robots that pick orders would be tested on nights first. I'd want to be on the side that installs them.

say: I'd tell colleagues now is the time to **get trained**, not hide.
I'd say companies should fund **training** from what the software saves them.
think: The **thinking work** like order planning and substitutions goes first, not my till.
Picking **robots on rails** would likely be tested on nights first.
do: Ask this month to **shadow the engineer** who services the self-checkouts.
Finish an **IT support certificate** within a year.
Use AI to rebuild my **CV** beyond shop work.
feel: **Uneasy**, but also **excited** to learn the new rules young.
S1.quote: My till isn't the first thing to go, the thinking work is. The robots that pick orders would be tested on nights first.
fieldNote: Adam reads the **order of change** clearly: software planning first, rail robots later.
He worries for older night staff like **Mick** more than himself.
His adaptability shows in **concrete moves**: shadowing, a certificate and a new CV within a year.

steps.text: Shadow the store engineer who services self-checkouts
Finish an IT support certificate within twelve months
Use an AI tool to rebuild the CV properly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud: the people who own the robots owe the rest of us. I'd be pushing for some kind of basic income, and I'd say that at work, even to managers. Online I'd stop being the cheerful tech guy for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this one shakes me. In 2028 the thinking AI wipes out the office jobs, so suddenly there are thousands of people applying for the IT and engineer roles I was aiming at. Then around 2031 the shelf and till robots arrive, and my fallback is gone too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fast in the two years before 2028. I'd try to get hired by the company that installs the robots, as a junior technician, even on lower pay, because being inside that firm beats being outside it. I'd push savings hard, maybe two hundred a month, and cut the gaming subscriptions and takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm usually the one telling people to chill, and here I'd be the one awake at four in the morning, which I already am, but for different reasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why join the robot company rather than fight it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the robots are coming either way in this picture, and somebody has to install and fix them. Better that it's someone like me who knows what a shop floor is like at night. I'd still argue for the union inside that firm, I'm not switching sides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your flatmate Dev, who works on screens all day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev's in a worse spot than me, honestly. My flatmate Dev is a coder, so in 2028 Dev's job is gone, while I'd have three more years of hands-on work. I've joked for years that he'd outlast me, and this picture flips it.

say: I'd say the **robot owners** owe everyone else and push for **basic income**.
I'd stop being the cheerful **tech guy** online for a while.
think: After 2028, laid-off office workers flood the **technician roles** I'm aiming at.
Shelf and till **robots around 2031** remove my fallback too.
do: Apply to the **robot installer** as a junior technician, even on lower pay.
Push savings to about **£200 a month** before 2028.
Cut **gaming subscriptions** and takeaways straight away.
feel: **Anxious** and awake at night for once, though he's usually the calm one.
S2.quote: My flatmate Dev is a coder, so in 2028 Dev's job is gone, while I'd have three more years of hands-on work.
fieldNote: Adam sees the **three-year gap** as useful, but fears competition for technical jobs.
His politics sharpen into support for a **basic income** when the timeline shortens.
He'd join the **robot firm** pragmatically, a tension with his union views.

steps.text: Apply as junior technician at the self-checkout installer
Save two hundred a month before 2028
Cancel gaming subscriptions and weekly takeaways
Sign and share the petition for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's not waste them arguing about whether it's real. At work I'd start a group chat for anyone wanting to learn the new kit. And I'd still say the companies should pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is decent. If the till and shelf robots come around 2034, I'd be thirty-five, with maybe five years as a technician behind me. It's still a race against everyone else retraining, but I'd have a head start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the IT certificate this year, then apply for the engineer apprenticeship the chain runs at head office. I'd keep about a hundred and fifty a month going into savings. And I'd use AI daily to practise fault-finding, because you can basically ask it to quiz you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but focused. More like a deadline than a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a head start actually look like for you by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It looks like a van with my name on the rota. By 2031 I'd want to be the person they call when a self-checkout or a picking robot breaks, with two years of call-outs behind me. That's a real job, not just a hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still back the union if you became a technician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, more than ever. Technicians get squeezed too. I'd want the union in the room before the first robot is wheeled into the supermarket. They'll have us on call at weird hours fixing robots for half what we're worth.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough if nobody wastes it arguing.
I'd start a work **group chat** for anyone learning the new kit.
think: Robots around **2034** means I could have years as a **technician** behind me.
It's still a **race** against everyone else retraining.
do: Finish the **IT certificate** this year, then apply for the chain's engineer apprenticeship.
Use AI daily as a **fault-finding quiz** to practise.
S3.quote: Technicians get squeezed too. I'd want the union in the room before the first robot is wheeled into the supermarket.
fieldNote: With five years, Adam's plan becomes a **clear ladder**: certificate, apprenticeship, technician.
He keeps his **union loyalty** even in the job he's aiming for.
His own income looks **secure for now**, so the worry is about others and the race.

steps.text: Apply to the chain's engineer apprenticeship after the certificate
Practise fault-finding with an AI quiz every day
Save a hundred and fifty a month
Start a staff group chat linked to the union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it to fix training and pensions properly. With friends I'd be pretty upbeat. Online I'd be the guy posting long threads about what governments should do with the decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's about the maths. Shop-floor robots around 2039 means I'd be forty. By then I could have a whole technical career. Maybe I'd even be running a team that looks after the machines. The scary part is all the people who think ten years means they can ignore it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the IT certificate, then a proper electrical engineering course part-time over a few years. I'd keep the night job while studying, because the pay is a bit better at night. I'd also try a side gig setting up smart home stuff for neighbours, just to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Kind of looking forward to it, if I'm honest, as long as it's shared fairly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the side gig actually be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Setting up video doorbells, smart lights and Wi-Fi for older people on my street, for twenty or thirty quid a job. My neighbour Mrs Okafor already asks me to fix her phone every week. It's not about the money really, it's practice with wires and real customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't it a bit easy to say ten years is a gift at twenty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. If I were fifty-five like Mick, ten years would just mean watching the clock. But I'm not, and I'd rather be honest that this one is good for me than pretend to be worried.

I'd post **long threads** on what governments should do with the decade.
think: Shop-floor robots around **2039** means I'd have a whole **technical career** by forty.
The danger is people who think a decade means they can **ignore it**.

Keep the **night job** for its better pay while studying.
Try a **side gig** setting up smart home kit for neighbours.
feel: Mostly **calm**, even **looking forward** to it if it's shared fairly.
S4.quote: Shop-floor robots around 2039 means I'd be forty. By then I could have a whole technical career.
fieldNote: Adam is honest that the **long timeline** favours him at twenty-seven.
He contrasts himself with older colleague **Mick** when challenged.
His **side gig** idea is about learning, not money.

steps.text: Study electrical engineering part-time over three years
Keep the better-paid night shifts while studying
Set up smart doorbells and lights for neighbours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the technical jobs I'm aiming for would be swamped by office people who lost their jobs first. What would help is apprenticeships that actually pay a living wage, so people like me can switch without starving. And some say for workers in how the robots get rolled out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who fixes the robots. Everyone talks about who loses their job, nobody talks about who's on call at three in the morning when the shelf robot falls over. That could be me, and I'd like it to be a decent job.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about who loses their job, nobody talks about who's on call at three in the morning when the shelf robot falls over.
portrait: Adam is **27**, a junior night cashier and online order picker at a **24-hour hypermarket**.
He shares a flat with Dev, a coder, and uses **AI tools daily** for budgeting and emails.
He wants to become the **technician** who fixes the self-checkouts and robots.
He backs **unions** and a basic income, yet would join the robot firm to stay inside.
Only **AGI by 2028** truly shakes him; longer timelines read as a ladder.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because laid-off office workers would swamp the technical jobs he's aiming for.
whatWouldHelp: A **worker voice** in how robots get rolled out.
